knowledge_point.title: Writing a Linear System of Differential Equations in Matrix Form

question.:question/problem:
$$ \displaystyle \left\{ \begin{array}{l}{x}_{1}^{\prime } ( t ) - {x}_{1} ( t ) - 5 {x}_{2} ( t ) = 2 \ln ( t ) \\ {x}_{2}^{\prime } ( t ) + 2 {x}_{2} ( t ) = - {t}^{2}\end{array} \right. $$ The system of linear ODEs above can be written in matrix form as follows:
$x^{′}(t) =$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-4}}{{field-5}}
$x(t) +$
{{field-3}}
{{field-6}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of equations that takes the following standard form:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) &=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) &=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where

- $a(t),$ $b(t),$ $c(t),$ $d(t),$ $f(t),$ and $g(t)$ are known functions, and

- ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are unknown functions (dependent variables).

Such a system can always be written in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

where

$$
x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix},\,A=\begin{bmatrix}a(t) & b(t) \\ c(t) & d(t)\end{bmatrix},\,f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}f(t) \\ g(t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We have the following system.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{\prime}(t)-{x}_{1}(t)-5{x}_{2}(t) &=2\ln(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{\prime}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) &=-t^{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Writing our system in standard form, we get the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{\prime}(t) &={x}_{1}(t)+5{x}_{2}(t)+2\ln(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{\prime}(t) &=-2{x}_{2}(t)-t^{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we can rewrite our system in matrix form as follows:

$$
x^{\prime}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}2\ln(t) \\ -t^{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$2^{D/3} =$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}$0$
$0${{field-4}}$0$$0$
$0$$0${{field-5}}$0$
$0$$0$$0${{field-6}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ with diagonal entries ${\lambda }_{1},…,{\lambda }_{n},$ we have

$$
f(D)=\begin{bmatrix}f({\lambda }_{1}) & ⋯ & 0 \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & f({\lambda }_{n})\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Here, the function is $f(z)=2^{z/3}$. Therefore, we have

$$
2^{D/3}=\begin{bmatrix}2^{3/3} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2^{-12/3} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2^{9/3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2^{21/3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{16} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 128\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Lotka-Volterra Model

question.:question/problem:
$$ \displaystyle \left\{ \begin{array}{l}{x}^{\prime } = x - 0.5 x y \\ {y}^{\prime } = - 0.2 y + 2 x y\end{array} \right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x = x(t)$ represents the prey and $y = y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium $x^{∗} = [0.1, 2]^{T}$, we get
$J(x^{∗}) =$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=x-0.5xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-0.2y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x}&=1-0.5y, & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial y}&=-0.5x, \\ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x}&=2y, & \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial y}&=-0.2+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}1-0.5y & -0.5x \\ 2y & -0.2+2x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^{\ast}=\begin{bmatrix}0.1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J(\mathbf{x}^{\ast})=\begin{bmatrix}1-0.5(2) & -0.5(0.1) \\ 2(2) & -0.2+2(0.1)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -0.05 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\det(J(\mathbf{x}^{\ast})-\lambda I)=\lambda^2+0.2=0.
$$

The eigenvalues are $\lambda_{1,2}=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,\mathrm{i}.$ For this classical Lotka–Volterra model, the positive coexistence equilibrium is a stable center. It is not asymptotically stable.

knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Stable Case

question.:question/problem:
$$ \displaystyle \left\{ \begin{array}{l}{x}^{\prime } = 2 x ( 1 - x ) - x y \\ {y}^{\prime } = - 2 y + 4 x y\end{array} \right. $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x = x(t)$ represents the prey and $y = y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below. Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium $x^{∗} = [1, 0]^{T}$, we get
$J(x^{∗}) =$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=2x(1-x)-xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-2y+4xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x}&=2-4x-y, & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial y}&=-x, \\ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x}&=4y, & \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial y}&=-2+4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2-4x-y & -x \\ 4y & -2+4x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^{\ast}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J(\mathbf{x}^{\ast})=\begin{bmatrix}2-4(1)-0 & -1 \\ 4(0) & -2+4(1)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\det(J(\mathbf{x}^{\ast})-\lambda I)=(-2-\lambda)(2-\lambda)=\lambda^2-4=0.
$$

The eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=-2$ and $\lambda_2=2.$ Since they are real with opposite signs, the equilibrium is an unstable saddle.

knowledge_point.title: Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Predator Extinction Case

question.:question/problem:

Select the correct options in the reasoning below. Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium $x^{∗} = [0.25, 0]^{T}$, we get
$J(x^{∗}) =$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=2x(1-4x)-xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-2y+4xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x}&=2-16x-y, & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial y}&=-x, \\ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x}&=4y, & \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial y}&=-2+4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2-16x-y & -x \\ 4y & -2+4x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^{\ast}=\begin{bmatrix}0.25 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J(\mathbf{x}^{\ast})=\begin{bmatrix}2-16(0.25)-0 & -0.25 \\ 4(0) & -2+4(0.25)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -0.25 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\det(J(\mathbf{x}^{\ast})-\lambda I)=(-2-\lambda)(-1-\lambda)=\lambda^2+3\lambda+2=0.
$$

The eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=-2$ and $\lambda_2=-1.$ Since both are real and negative, the equilibrium is an asymptotically stable sink.

question.:question/problem:
Given the function $f(x; w) = w_{1}x_{1} + w_{2}x_{2}$, compute $∇_{w}f$ with the input $x = [2,-1]^{T}$.
$∇_{w}f =$
{{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
To compute $\nabla_{w}f$, we take partial derivatives with respect to each component of $w.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial w_{1}} &=\frac{\partial}{\partial w_{1}}(w_{1}x_{1}+w_{2}x_{2})=x_{1} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial w_{2}} &=\frac{\partial}{\partial w_{2}}(w_{1}x_{1}+w_{2}x_{2})=x_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, with $x=[2,-1]^{T}$, we obtain the following:

$$
\nabla_{w}f=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find $e^{At}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}$. *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1 ± 2\textrm{i}$.*
$e^{At} = e^{t}$
$\cos (2t) + \sin (2t)${{field-1}}
$\sin (2t)${{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{At} &= \alpha_1At+\alpha_0I \\ &=\alpha_1\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}t+\alpha_0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha_{0} + 3 \alpha_{1} t & - 4 \alpha_{1} t \\ 2 \alpha_{1} t & \alpha_{0} - \alpha_{1} t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda)=\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are $t \left(1 + 2 i\right)$ and $t \left(1 - 2 i\right)$, which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t \left(1 + 2 i\right))&=e^{t \left(1 + 2 i\right)} \\ t \left(1 + 2 i\right)\alpha_1+\alpha_0&=e^{t}\bigl(\cos{\left(2 t \right)}+\mathrm{i}\sin{\left(2 t \right)}\bigr)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha_{0} + \alpha_{1} t&=e^{t} \cos{\left(2 t \right)} \\ 2 \alpha_{1} t&=e^{t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} \\ \alpha_1&=\frac{e^{t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2 t} \\ \alpha_0&=\left(- \frac{\sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\right) e^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the required entries of $e^{At}$, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}- 4 \alpha_{1} t &=- 2 e^{t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)} \\ &=e^{t}\bigl(-2\sin(2t)\bigr) \\ \alpha_{0} - \alpha_{1} t &=\left(- \frac{\sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} + \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\right) e^{t} - \frac{e^{t} \sin{\left(2 t \right)}}{2} \\ &=e^{t}\bigl(\cos(2t)-\sin(2t)\bigr)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
e^{At}=e^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\sin{\left(2 t \right)} + \cos{\left(2 t \right)} & - 2 \sin{\left(2 t \right)} \\ \sin{\left(2 t \right)} & - \sin{\left(2 t \right)} + \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The coefficient $\alpha_1$ at $t=0$ is understood by continuity; the final matrix formula holds for every real $t$.

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find $e^{At}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}$. *Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $3$, and it has multiplicity two.*
$e^{At} = e^{3t}$
{{field-1}}$2t$
{{field-2}}$2t + 1$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{At} &= \alpha_1At+\alpha_0I \\ &=\alpha_1\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 5\end{bmatrix}t+\alpha_0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha_{0} + \alpha_{1} t & 2 \alpha_{1} t \\ - 2 \alpha_{1} t & \alpha_{0} + 5 \alpha_{1} t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda)=\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is $3 t$, of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3 t)&=e^{3 t} \\ r\,^{\prime}(3 t)&=e^{3 t} \\ \alpha_{0} + 3 \alpha_{1} t&=e^{3 t} \\ \alpha_1&=e^{3 t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$:

- From the second equation, we get

$$
\alpha_1=e^{3 t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
3 t e^{3 t}+\alpha_0=e^{3 t}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\alpha_0=\left(1 - 3 t\right) e^{3 t}.
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the required entries of $e^{At}$, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha_{0} + \alpha_{1} t &=t e^{3 t} + \left(1 - 3 t\right) e^{3 t} \\ &=e^{3 t}\bigl(1-2t\bigr) \\ - 2 \alpha_{1} t &=- 2 t e^{3 t} \\ &=e^{3 t}\bigl(-2t\bigr)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
e^{At}=e^{3 t}\begin{bmatrix}1 - 2 t & 2 t \\ - 2 t & 2 t + 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Linear Approximations Near Equilibria

question.:question/problem:
$$ \displaystyle \left\{ \begin{array}{l}{x}^{\prime } ( t ) = {x}^{2} ( t ) - y ( t ) \\ {y}^{\prime } ( t ) = 3 x ( t ) + {y}^{2} ( t )\end{array} \right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point $x^{∗} = [0, 0]^{T}$?
$u^{′} =$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$u$
, where $u = x - x^{∗}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as

$$
\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix},\qquad \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{bmatrix}x^2-y \\ 3x+y^2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\boldsymbol{f}.$ First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x}&=2x, & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial y}&=-1, \\ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x}&=3, & \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial y}&=2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2x & -1 \\ 3 & 2y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^{\ast}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J(\mathbf{x}^{\ast})=\begin{bmatrix}2(0) & -1 \\ 3 & 2(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
\mathbf{u}^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{u},
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\ast}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Linear Approximations Near Equilibria

question.:question/problem:
$$ \displaystyle \left\{ \begin{array}{l}{x}^{\prime } ( t ) = {x}^{2} ( t ) - x ( t ) + 2 y ( t ) - 4 \\ {y}^{\prime } ( t ) = - 3 x ( t ) + {y}^{2} ( t ) - 4 y ( t ) + 7\end{array} \right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point $x^{∗} = [1, 2]^{T}$?
$u^{′} =$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$u$
, where $u = x - x^{∗}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as

$$
\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix},\qquad \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{bmatrix}x^2-x+2y-4 \\ -3x+y^2-4y+7\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\boldsymbol{f}.$ First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x}&=2x-1, & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial y}&=2, \\ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x}&=-3, & \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial y}&=2y-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2x-1 & 2 \\ -3 & 2y-4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium $\mathbf{x}^{\ast}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J(\mathbf{x}^{\ast})=\begin{bmatrix}2(1)-1 & 2 \\ -3 & 2(2)-4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
\mathbf{u}^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{u},
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\ast}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y-2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Real Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find $e^{At}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}$. *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $-3$ and $2$.*
$e^{At} = \frac{1}{5}$
{{field-1}}$6e^{2t} - 6e^{-3t}$
{{field-2}}$2e^{2t} + 3e^{-3t}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{At} &= \alpha_1At+\alpha_0I \\ &=\alpha_1\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}t+\alpha_0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha_{0} & 6 \alpha_{1} t \\ \alpha_{1} t & \alpha_{0} - \alpha_{1} t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda)=\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are $- 3 t$ and $2 t$, both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(- 3 t)&=e^{- 3 t} \\ r(2 t)&=e^{2 t} \\ \alpha_{0} - 3 \alpha_{1} t&=e^{- 3 t} \\ \alpha_{0} + 2 \alpha_{1} t&=e^{2 t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$:

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
5 \alpha_{1} t=e^{2 t} - e^{- 3 t}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\alpha_1=\frac{e^{2 t} - e^{- 3 t}}{5 t}.
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and the second by $3$, then adding, we get

$$
5\alpha_0=3 e^{2 t} + 2 e^{- 3 t}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\alpha_0=\frac{3 e^{2 t}}{5} + \frac{2 e^{- 3 t}}{5}.
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the required entries of $e^{At}$, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha_{0} &=\frac{3 e^{2 t}}{5} + \frac{2 e^{- 3 t}}{5} \\ &=\frac{1}{5}\bigl(3e^{2t}+2e^{-3t}\bigr) \\ \alpha_{1} t &=\frac{e^{2 t}}{5} - \frac{e^{- 3 t}}{5} \\ &=\frac{1}{5}\bigl(e^{2t}-e^{-3t}\bigr)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
e^{At}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}3 e^{2 t} + 2 e^{- 3 t} & 6 e^{2 t} - 6 e^{- 3 t} \\ e^{2 t} - e^{- 3 t} & 2 e^{2 t} + 3 e^{- 3 t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The coefficient $\alpha_1$ at $t=0$ is understood by continuity; the final matrix formula holds for every real $t$.

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find $e^{At}$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}$. *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $± \textrm{i}$.*
$e^{At} =$
{{field-1}}$\sin (t)$
{{field-2}}$\cos (t) - \sin (t)$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}e^{At} &= \alpha_1At+\alpha_0I \\ &=\alpha_1\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}t+\alpha_0\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha_{0} + \alpha_{1} t & \alpha_{1} t \\ - 2 \alpha_{1} t & \alpha_{0} - \alpha_{1} t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda)=\alpha_1\lambda+\alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are $i t$ and $- i t$, which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(i t)&=e^{i t} \\ i t\alpha_1+\alpha_0&=1\bigl(\cos{\left(t \right)}+\mathrm{i}\sin{\left(t \right)}\bigr)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha_{0}&=\cos{\left(t \right)} \\ \alpha_{1} t&=\sin{\left(t \right)} \\ \alpha_1&=\frac{\sin{\left(t \right)}}{t} \\ \alpha_0&=\cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the required entries of $e^{At}$, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha_{0} + \alpha_{1} t &=\sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)} \\ &=\cos(t)+\sin(t) \\ - 2 \alpha_{1} t &=- 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} \\ &=-2\sin(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
e^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)} & \sin{\left(t \right)} \\ - 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} & - \sin{\left(t \right)} + \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The coefficient $\alpha_1$ at $t=0$ is understood by continuity; the final matrix formula holds for every real $t$.

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues

${e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\,\,$

question.:question/worked-solution:

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =3{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1+t), \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{2t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\begin{bmatrix}1+t & t \\ -t & 1-t\end{bmatrix}.
$$
